structured_output.summary: I looked for outside evidence on the open nodes: late freeze (H2.20, H2.21), depth cuts (H2.18), group-3 width (H2.19), Muon variants (H7) and the systems levers. Public CIFAR-100 speedrun repos publish no leaderboard beyond the 75.36% / 59.30 s baseline. The futurebiohackers repo now returns 404. The most useful find is FreezeOut. It anneals each layer's LR to zero at that layer's own freeze point. Its ResNets saved ~20% with no accuracy loss, and the measured speedup was 1.3x the FLOP prediction, which is independent support for H2.21's claim that the high-res early layers cost more than their FLOP share. FreezeOut also skips BN statistics in frozen layers. That suggests two cheap untested refinements of E116: anneal group 1's LR to 0 at the freeze point instead of a hard detach, and run the frozen group-1 BN in eval mode, folded into the conv. MosaicML's freezing card is the counterweight: about 5% throughput and no Pareto gain. On depth (H2.18), airbench95 is the 2-conv-per-block reference (128/384/384, 15 epochs, 95.01% on CIFAR-10). No published same-epoch ablation of 2 vs 3 convs exists, and airbench's own FLOP cut (first-conv kernel 3->2, -20% FLOPs) gave no A100 wall-time gain. E123 has already measured real wall-time gains, so the open question there is accuracy. On H2.19, futurebiohackers chose 576 from a ~40-config sweep, noting that widening the last block 'adds accuracy for little compute'. That lowers the prior that a 512 cut (-5.2%, E117) is cheap in accuracy. New directions not yet in the tree: stochastic depth on the residual branches as a dose-controlled depth cut (low prior here), and NorMuon's row-wise normalization (LM-only evidence, low prior). Fable's write-up confirms that whole-run CUDA graphs and fusion gain only ~5 ms, consistent with the closed H2.14/H3 levers.

findings.claim: FreezeOut freezes layers one by one. Each layer's LR is cosine-annealed to zero at its own freeze time: alpha_i(t)=0.5*alpha_i(0)*(1+cos(pi t/t_i)). Freeze times are linearly spaced from t0 to the end, or cubed for the cubic schedule. Recommended settings are cubic with LR scaling (t0=0.8, alpha_i(0)=alpha/t_i) or linear without scaling (t0=0.5). Reported results: ~20% wall-clock saving with no accuracy loss on (Wide) ResNets, ~20% with a 3% loss on DenseNets, and no improvement on VGG. The authors suggest skip connections matter. For linear scheduling, the FLOP-based speedup prediction underestimated the real speedup, and multiplying it by 1.3 fixed the gap. Frozen layers' BN no longer computes means and variances.
findings.relevance: This is independent support that freezing early layers saves more wall time than its FLOP share (the 1.3x factor), matching E116/E122. The per-layer LR anneal to 0 at the freeze point differs from E116's hard detach at a nonzero LR and might shrink the -0.09 pp freeze loss. Skipping BN statistics in frozen layers is an extra saving E116 did not take.

findings.claim: Layer freezing gives ~5% throughput on ResNet-50/ImageNet at a 0.5-1% accuracy loss. On ResNet-56/CIFAR-100, accuracy rose from 75.82% to 76.22% with ~5% speed gain. The card says there is 'no evidence that layer freezing improves the tradeoff between model quality and training speed': it did not improve the Pareto frontier. It recommends freeze_start >= 0.1.
findings.relevance: This prior is consistent with E116 and E120: a real rate lever, not a free one. The CIFAR-100 point shows that a small or positive accuracy effect is possible at mild freezing.

findings.claim: Egeria freezes converged front layers to skip their backward. It also caches the frozen layers' intermediate outputs, with prefetching, to skip their forward, reporting a 19-43% training speedup without accuracy loss.
findings.relevance: Forward caching does not transfer here. The frozen window is ~0.4 epoch, each image is seen at most once in it, and augmentation is fresh each time. What remains of the 'make the frozen forward cheaper' idea is BN eval mode plus folding into the conv (see the FreezeOut finding).

findings.claim: Setting requires_grad=False does not stop a BN layer from updating its running stats. A fully frozen BN layer needs .eval() so it uses running statistics instead of batch statistics.
findings.relevance: This is an untested refinement of the E116 freeze, which keeps group-1 BN in train mode. In the frozen window, put stem + group-1 BN in eval mode (or fold it into the conv weights). The batch-stat reduction passes over the 31x31x128 activations then disappear from the forward. The accuracy risk is low, because running stats track the batch closely (momentum ~0.4/step, E018). The expected gain is small, a fraction of the ~15% window, so this is likely <0.5% of total time. It needs its own warmed graph variant.

findings.claim: airbench95 keeps 2 convs per block, widens to 128/384/384 channels and trains 15 epochs: 95.01% in 10.4 A100-seconds, 1.4e15 FLOPs. airbench96 adds a third conv per block with a residual across the last two convs, widths 128/512/512, plus Cutout and 40 epochs: 96.05% in 46.3 s. The paper also notes that cutting the first conv's kernel in each block from 3 to 2, plus 5 more epochs, lowers FLOPs by almost 20% but does not improve A100 wall time.
findings.relevance: airbench95 is the external 2-conv reference for depth cuts. No published same-epoch ablation of 2 vs 3 convs exists, so the accuracy cost of E123's group-1-conv3 or group-3-conv3 removal (-7.6%/-6.1% projected) must be measured here. The kernel-size result shows FLOP cuts often fail on A100, but E123 already measured a real wall-time gain.

findings.claim: Search snippet; the repo now returns 404. The futurebiohackers defaults (3-conv groups 128/384/576, LS 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs) came from ~40 configs swept on Modal A100s. They report that widening the last block (7x7 and 3x3 spatial) 'adds accuracy for little compute', and that LS 0.3 beat 0.2 and 0.4.
findings.relevance: 576 was chosen because group-3 width bought CIFAR-100 accuracy, so cutting to 512 (E117: -5.2% projected, FLOP-proportional) probably costs accuracy beyond E117's 0.15 pp bar. That lowers the prior for scoring the 512 arm.

findings.claim: Stochastic depth on ResNet-110 (drop rate 0.5, linear decay with depth) cut training time by 25% and changed accuracy by +1.2 pp on CIFAR-10, +2.8 pp on CIFAR-100 and -0.2 pp on ImageNet. Skipped residual blocks bypass both forward and backward.
findings.relevance: New direction, not in the tree: a dose-controlled alternative to H2.18's hard depth cut. Randomly skip the residual branch (conv2-conv3) of group 1 or group 3 per batch with probability p, keeping the full net at test time. The prior is low here: the gains come from 110-layer nets with long schedules, our net has only 3 residual branches, and every skip pattern needs a warmed static graph variant. Consider it only if the hard depth cut (E123 variants) costs too much accuracy.

findings.claim: Drop-Muon updates only a randomized subset of layers per step and reaches the same accuracy up to 1.4x faster in wall-clock time in controlled CNN experiments. The paper argues full-network updates are optimal only under a specific relation between layer smoothness constants.
findings.relevance: This weakly supports the stochastic/progressive freeze arm. The evidence comes from small controlled CNNs, not tuned speedrun recipes, so H2.20.3's low prior stands.

findings.claim: NorMuon applies row-wise (per-neuron) normalization, using second-moment statistics, after Muon's orthogonalization. It fixes the non-uniform neuron norms that orthogonalization leaves and reports an 11.31% training-efficiency gain over Muon in 1.1B LM pretraining. No CNN or CIFAR results are reported.
findings.relevance: A possible zero-time accuracy arm under H7 that the tree has not considered. The cost is a per-row second-moment buffer inside the compiled update. The prior is low: the evidence is LM-only, our filters feed BN and are renormed, and every Muon scalar knob has come back flat.

findings.claim: Fable's write-up: a 24 px step does 0.56x the arithmetic of a 32 px step. The 28->32 curriculum saved 0.128 s and extending it to 24->28->32 saved another 0.081 s. Capturing the whole ~284-step run as one CUDA graph gained only ~5 ms, because the net is not launch-bound. The full systems stack was ~0.04 s slower than plain torch.compile on the equivalent curriculum.
findings.relevance: This confirms the tree's closure of CUDA-graph and fusion levers (H2.12, H3, H2.14). On CIFAR-10, Fable found nothing systems-side beyond progressive resizing and pooling.

findings.claim: hiverge's 1.99 s CIFAR-10 record changed GELU to SiLU, initialized whitening via SVD, batched Muon over padded matrices, compiled fwd/bwd, added brightness/contrast augmentation and selective TTA, and retuned steps, LR and momentum. No per-change gains are published.
findings.relevance: Nothing new transfers. SiLU and brightness/contrast were already refuted here (E003, E008), and TTA is forbidden by the rules.

findings.claim: Turbo-Muon (AOL-preconditioned orthogonalization) gave identical accuracy on a CIFAR-10 speedrun, with runtime falling from 1.359 s to 1.348 s (-0.81%).
findings.relevance: Even a well-engineered cheaper orthogonalizer saves <1% on a CIFAR speedrun, which confirms the closure of H7.2 and the retirement of H7.2.4.

findings.claim: The public CIFAR-100 speedrun framework repos (RyanChong0117, Daniel-T-S-Adams) list only the organizer's ResNet9-style baseline: 75.36% in 59.30 s (40 epochs, width 64, A100 PCIe). They publish no leaderboard or competitor techniques.
findings.relevance: There is no outside CIFAR-100 recipe to mine for accuracy sources. The tip at ~4.26 s (population mean ~0.7521) is far ahead of any published CIFAR-100 number.
